svg.text: WOTS+C: constant sum in place of a checksum
What is signed: a 32-byte digest, cut into 32 digits of 4 bits each, at w = 16
Key generation
32 chains, and no checksum chains at all.
sₖ = PRF(sk_seed, ADRS)
pₖ = H¹⁵(sₖ)
public key = T(p₀ ‖ p₁ ‖ … ‖ p₃₁), one 16-byte value
WOTS-TW would need 35 chains here;
the 3 saved are 48 bytes per signature.
Signing
The digits are not taken from the digest directly. The signer
grinds a 16-bit counter until they happen to sum to 240:
d = base_2b(H_grind(pk_seed, ADRS, digest, i), 4, 32)
stop when Σ dₖ = 240, and the counter i joins the signature
The 32 digits of one real signature, at counter 22
each bar is how far along its chain that digit sits, out of 15
Chain 6 in full, signing the digit 8
signer walks d = 8
verifier walks 15 − d = 7
sₖ
σₖ in the signature
pₖ
Verification
1. recompute the digits from the counter in the signature
2. reject at once if they do not sum to 240
3. from each σₖ, walk the remaining 15 − dₖ steps
accept iff the 32 chain ends compress to the public key
The property this buys
The verifier walks exactly 240 chain steps, for every
message. Worst case and average are the same number.
Why a fixed sum works where a checksum did
A forgery still means raising some digit. But the digits are admitted only if they
sum to 240, so raising one forces lowering another, and lowering means walking
that chain backwards. The constraint does what the checksum chain did, for free.
What the search costs
P(Σ = 240) ≈ 0.0152, so about 66 counters
on average. All 2¹⁶ failing has probability
below 2⁻¹⁴⁵⁰; the signer then falls back.
The cost lands on the signer, which is the right side of the trade.
Grinding is roughly 66 extra hashes, paid once per signature. Verification happens on every node, for every block, forever,
and it is verification that a consensus rule has to price for the worst case it can be handed.
